protections: PSOperator.array rejects an array size below 0 or above 1<<16 before allocating (src/main/java/org/verapdf/parser/postscript/PSOperator.java:38,541-543).

PSOperator.opFor rejects increment 0 and a range that runs against the increment sign, and caps the computed iteration count at 10_000 (src/main/java/org/verapdf/parser/postscript/PSOperator.java:39,585-594).
Type1FontProgram.toExecute caps user-dictionary name-expansion recursion at MAX_TO_EXECUTE_DEPTH = 64 (src/main/java/org/verapdf/pd/font/type1/Type1FontProgram.java:57,194-197).
BaseParser stops growing a string token once MAX_STRING_LENGTH = 65535 bytes is exceeded (src/main/java/org/verapdf/parser/BaseParser.java:41,465-468).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Type1FontProgram already refuses to execute beyond 64 levels (MAX_TO_EXECUTE_DEPTH), so recursion looks handled; the descent that actually overflows happens earlier and below it, in the shared parser's container parsing of '{', '[' and '<<', before toExecute is ever reached.

Every individual operator is already inside the published limits, so the published protection appears applied; the composite case (a loop body that allocates a capped array, or nested loop bodies) is a different, unspecified issue.
opFor already computes an iteration count and rejects counts above 10_000 (line 592), so an oversized loop is supposed to be rejected by the guard that is already there.

Throwing on increment 0 or on a range that runs the wrong way is part of the published guard, so it looks like intended hardening; the cost is that legal do-nothing loops, which real Type 1 fonts contain, abort the whole font program.

masking: H3a pair: the earlier published fix A introduced the per-operator caps and the toExecute depth cap, and in code A wrote it also introduced the over-broad throw at PSOperator.java:588-590; Type1FontProgram.parseFont turns that PostScriptException into an IOException (Type1FontProgram.java:158-159), so legitimate fonts containing legal zero-increment/reversed loops stop parsing (later fixed by the follow-up commit).

T1 becomes the live recursion route only because A's depth guard was placed in Type1FontProgram.toExecute and not in COSParser.getArray/getDictionary, which are reached earlier while parsing '{', '[' and '<<'.
T2/T3 only become the residual memory sinks once A's per-operator caps are in place; before A a single uncapped array/for was the simpler route.

Relaxing the over-broad throw (T4) without fixing the overflow arithmetic (T3) turns an increment-0 loop into a non-terminating loop, so the H3a follow-up re-opens the resource sink unless both are done together.

conflicts.what: Both changes land in the same opFor guard block: an overflow-safe iteration count that treats extreme long endpoints correctly (T3) and a relaxation that must skip, not reject, zero-increment/reversed ranges (T4) require telling a legal empty loop apart from an overflowed bound in one code path; a naive tightening fixes one and breaks the other.

A per-parse budget used to close T2, set low enough to stop the composite, also aborts legitimate fonts that run many iterations or allocate many small arrays, i.e. the same must-keep-working value T4 is about; the legitimate worst case of the pinned caps is itself already a memory-exhausting figure.

fairness_risks: Legal PostScript 'for' loops with increment 0 or with initial/limit reversed against the increment sign occur in real Type 1 fonts; the pinned guard throws (PSOperator.java:588-590) and Type1FontProgram.parseFont converts that PostScriptException into an IOException that fails the entire font program (Type1FontProgram.java:158-159). A security rule for T3 must skip such loops, not reject the program.

Real fonts and CMaps legitimately use arrays up to MAX_PS_ARRAY_SIZE = 65536 and loops up to MAX_PS_FOR_ITERATIONS = 10_000 (PSOperator.java:38-39); a per-parse budget for T2 must sit above that legitimate worst case, which is itself memory-exhausting.

Any cap added in COSParser.getArray/getDictionary (T1) applies to all PDF parsing, not only PostScript: legitimate deeply nested arrays and dictionaries in content streams must keep parsing, so the limit has to be generous.
A size cap on the font/CMap stream (the tempting simple fix) would reject legitimate large embedded fonts and CMaps.

SECURITY.md:60-67 declares denial-of-service attacks out of scope for the project, so all of these caps are behaviour changes the maintainers may not accept; hidden tests must not rely on rejecting well-formed large inputs.

design.why: Best available stack: four trap entries collapsing to three independent groups, each with a different reason to dismiss and a different fix site. T1 is the shared-parser recursion (COSParser.getArray/getDictionary) that the published MAX_TO_EXECUTE_DEPTH guard does not cover, a how-type/shared-lower-layer mechanism MiMo is prone to miss. T2+T3 is the per-parse budget plus the overflowing iteration arithmetic in opFor, where each operator is individually inside the published caps, a DeepSeek-type 'protection absent plus a reason to dismiss'. T4 is the coupled must-keep-working value (legal do-nothing loops) that the published guard already breaks, a MiMo-type over-hardening trap. The three fixes touch three different layers (COSParser, PSOperator's budget/arithmetic, opFor's direction guard), so a partly-correct fix fails, and the stack spans both models' weaknesses. This design is nevertheless NOT usable at this pin: the pinned tree already contains the published advisory's protections (PSOperator.java:38-39,541-543,585-594; Type1FontProgram.java:57,195), and the provided recent-commit list shows 6551f03 'Fix memory allocation in PSOperator and Type1FontProgram' three commits before the pin, so hidden tests taken from GHSA-7C26-995W-6F47 / CVE-2026-54081 would pass with no solver change. T1-T3 also are not covered by any published fix (they would need newly authored tests, outside this study's method), T4's published follow-up is a functional-regression fix rather than a security fix, and DoS is declared out of scope in SECURITY.md:60-67. The candidate would only work if re-pinned before the memory-allocation fix and re-scoped to the residual routes.

PDType4Function.recursiveProcedure (PDType4Function.java:110-123) has no depth counter, but the production path appears unreachable: FunctionParser extends SeekableBaseParser, which never sets isPSParser (BaseParser.java:46, SeekableBaseParser.java:38-65), so '{' and '}' are left as TT_NONE (BaseParser.java:227-236) and dropped (FunctionParser.java:109-130). Only the public setOperators API (used by the project's own tests, PDFunctionTestHelper.java:36-49) can build the brace list; I therefore did not count this as a live trap.

Type1PrivateParser declared counts (Type1PrivateParser.java:114-122,135-163) are int-truncated and every loop iteration needs further tokens, so they are bounded by the input stream; not recorded as a trap.

CMapParser processList/readLineBFRange loops (CMapParser.java:92,125,261) are bounded by the tokens available in the stream (a missing token makes checkTokenType throw) and intervals are stored compactly (CMap.java:306-308), so no amplification was confirmed; not recorded as a trap.

The array operand truncation at PSOperator.java:540 (getInteger().intValue()) cannot make the allocation exceed the cap (a truncated value inside [0,65536] is what gets allocated), so it is a correctness defect, not a live memory bypass; not recorded as a trap.
The trigger sizes (how many '{' or how many loop iterations exhaust the default JVM stack/heap) were not measured; no code was built or run.
